title: How To Have Better, Sharper Routines Next School Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin uses the example of an experienced teacher whose well-taught, well-modeled routines still felt laborious and prompted grumbling to illustrate a subtle but common problem: routines performed too slowly. He explains that routines should be executed as fast as possible without becoming sloppy, since a brisk pace adds an element of challenge that students find fulfilling and enjoyable, while a plodding pace drains energy and invites complaint. He notes the amount of modeling and number of routines needed should shrink as students get older, and that routine style should always be matched to grade level. His actionable recommendation is for teachers to try performing routines 10% faster in the coming year, pushing for the same precision expected in academic work but at a snappier pace, arguing this transforms routines from drudgery into a source of success and satisfaction.
points: A case study of an experienced teacher illustrates that even well-taught, well-modeled routines can fail if they are performed too slowly.
Routines should be executed as fast as possible without becoming sloppy; excessive slowness drains energy and invites complaint.
A brisk pace adds an element of challenge that students find fulfilling and enjoyable, changing their attitude toward performing routines.
The amount of modeling and number of routines needed decreases as students get older, and routine style should be matched to grade level.
The concrete recommendation is to try performing classroom routines about 10% faster in the coming school year.
quotes: Routines are the lifeblood of a well-run classroom. Because, done right, they save tons of learning time.
Her routines felt laborious. Her students would perform them, but reluctantly and often poorly. Every transition was becoming a downer and a drain on her patience.
The answer is a simple little thing, but it can be a very big deal: She was (and her students were) doing them too slow .
For routines to be most effective, for them to be sharp and efficient and for students to be motivated to perform them, they should be done as fast as possible without becoming sloppy .
It works because speeding them up adds an element of challenge, which is not only fulfilling and enjoyable for students, but it will change their perspective and attitude toward performing them.
So this coming school year, try performing your routines just 10% faster. Make em’ snappy.
